newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka detains four Danish journalists. [CORRECTED 10:55 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka detains four Danish journalists. [CORRECTED 10:55 GMT]

text.p: Sri Lankan police have detained four Danish journalists who were in Colombo to cover the case of a young Tamil refugee deported from Denmark earlier this month, a Danish diplomat said on Tuesday.
The four journalists were taken from their hotel rooms late on Saturday by the Crime Detective Bureau (CDB), Danish Consul General P.B. Rasmussen said.
"They have been taken in for questioning," he told Reuters by telephone. "We were sort of expecting them to be released yesterday," said Rasmussen, who said he now expected their release on Tuesday.

The release of the four -- Ole Hoff-Lund of the Berlingske Tidende newspaper, Morten Jastrup of Information newspaper, Nis Olsen of Politiken and Jens Moeller of Danish TV2 -- was held up as the CDB was waiting for instructions from the Ministry of Defence, he said (corrects names of journalists and their media organisations).
Rasmussen said he was able to contact the four on Monday by telephone at a seaside Colombo hotel, where they were being held under police guard.
The hotel declined to put reporters' calls through and the CDB was not immediately available for comment.
Sri Lanka's English-language daily newspaper The Island said the four were to be held through Friday under Emergency Regulations.
The journalists arrived in Colombo last week to follow the case of Chitra Rajendran, an 18-year-old Tamil refugee deported on November 2 from Denmark, where she had sought asylum three years ago.
The deportation caused an outcry among Danish human rights activists and the Tamil community in Denmark.

According to reports in the Sri Lankan press, Rajendran is under police detention in Colombo on suspicion of having links with the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), with whom two of her brothers are full time activists.
The LTTE is fighting a 14-year-old war for a separate Tamil state in the north and east of the island that has cost 50,000 lives, according to government estimates.
The LTTE says the death toll is much higher.

The government on October 8 lifted a six-month gag on news of the war, during which it censored all coverage of the conflict by local media, arguing that such measures were required to prevent the leak of military secrets.
Journalists' access to the north remains tightly restricted.
